content: Tuberculosis (TB) surveillance aims to provide an accurate measurement of the number of new TB cases and related deaths occurring annually, as well as to assess trends over time. While some countries have surveillance systems that meet the necessary standards, others face significant gaps that hinder accurate measurement. For instance, TB cases diagnosed in the private sector often go unreported, and in high-burden countries, many individuals with TB may not access healthcare and remain undiagnosed. Additionally, many countries lack vital registration systems with sufficient geographical coverage and quality to accurately measure TB-related deaths. To address these challenges, the World Health Organization (WHO) developed a checklist of standards and benchmarks for TB surveillance and vital registration systems. This checklist serves two primary objectives: to assess a national surveillance system's ability to accurately measure TB cases and deaths, and to identify gaps that need to be addressed to improve TB surveillance. The results of these assessments can help determine which countries already have robust surveillance systems and define the actions required to strengthen systems where gaps are identified. The checklist consists of two parts. Part A provides a general description of the TB surveillance system being assessed, while Part B includes specific standards and benchmarks. Part B is further divided into two sections: Section 1 focuses on data quality, system coverage, and TB mortality data from vital registration systems, while Section 2 includes supplementary standards for the surveillance of TB/HIV coinfection, drug-resistant TB, and childhood TB. Part A comprises 18 questions that characterize the national TB surveillance system, setting the context for Part B, which includes 13 standards and their associated benchmarks. The standards in the checklist are general statements outlining the criteria for a high-performance TB surveillance system. Nine standards pertain to the measurement of TB cases, and one pertains to the measurement of TB deaths. Additionally, three supplementary standards assess whether a national TB surveillance system can provide direct measurements of drug-resistant TB cases, HIV-positive TB cases, and childhood TB cases. Benchmarks are defined quantitatively wherever possible to indicate the level of performance required to meet the respective standards. The checklist is designed to use data from the most recent complete calendar year, unless otherwise specified. Depending on the timeliness of reporting and data validation, the lag time may range from no delay to up to one year. In some cases, data from additional years may be needed to assess trends, or data from a single quarter may suffice to reduce the burden of data collection. It is anticipated that assessments using the checklist would occur every three to five years. The checklist also provides a framework for identifying key actions to address gaps in surveillance and vital registration systems, improve data quality, and align with best practices. An estimated budget to support activities that bridge these gaps can assist in developing a monitoring and evaluation (M&E) investment plan. The user guide accompanying the checklist provides detailed instructions on how to implement the checklist accurately and systematically. It explains the rationale for each standard and benchmark, the methods for assessing benchmarks, and how to collect and review data. Examples are included to illustrate methods and recommended corrective actions if benchmarks are not met. Certification of a TB surveillance system requires meeting all 10 standards and their associated benchmarks in Part B, Section 1. The three supplementary standards in Part B, Section 2, can be used to assess whether the system provides direct and specific measures of drug-resistant TB cases, HIV-positive TB cases, and childhood TB cases. Certification provides an objective analysis of the current TB surveillance system, offering a baseline and framework for improvements. Subsequent assessments can determine whether targets are met based on the initial evaluation. Certification is based on a review of the system during the assessed time period and requires external peer review and endorsement by the WHO Global Task Force on TB Impact Measurement. The checklist can be used by in-country national TB program staff for self-assessment. It should be undertaken by individuals with informed and current knowledge of the system, such as national TB program managers, program officers, monitoring and evaluation officers, statisticians, epidemiologists, data managers, or WHO TB program officers. Completing the checklist requires accurate and thorough data collection from available sources, including a desktop review of documents, datasets, and electronic surveillance systems. Data audits at selected basic management units (BMUs) may also be necessary, along with interviews with relevant stakeholders and partners. The checklist focuses on assessing the outputs of the surveillance system rather than its inputs or processes, which vary by country. By identifying areas where additional resources can be targeted, countries can effectively strengthen their surveillance systems. The checklist may also be used at the sub-national level, although this is not its primary purpose.
